To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) there is a strong positive relationship between the amount of cortisol produced and the number of times an individual has been stressed in the past 6 months; (2) the amount of cortisol in the saliva of individuals who have recently been stressed is significantly greater than in those who have not been stressed recently; and (3) the amount of saliva cortisol in individuals who are stressed at present is significantly greater than that of individuals who are not stressed at present.

(1) cortisol is elevated in response to stress, but not in response to all stressors; (2) the magnitude of the cortisol response depends on the nature of the stressor, the individual’s interpretation of the stressor and his or her coping resources; (3) there are substantial differences in the magnitude of the response among individuals; and (4) the cortisol response is not always a good predictor of the subjective experience of stress.
the cortisol response to a social stressor is not related to the cortisol response to an acute physical stressor.

the cortisol response to stress is not a unitary phenomenon.
